sections.description: Walk the reader through the patient’s history, presentation, vital signs, physical findings, and the immediate ED response that established the working diagnosis of severe anaphylaxis.
subtopics: Relevant history: medication allergies (beta-lactams), comorbidities, new antibiotic exposures (clindamycin then first-ever clarithromycin)
Symptom timeline: onset 1 hour after clarithromycin; progressive pruritus, flushing, throat fullness; hypotension and hypoxemia on arrival
Diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis at presentation (acute skin/mucosal involvement plus respiratory compromise and hypotension)
Initial differential for shock and hypoxemia in this context (anaphylaxis vs sepsis, cardiogenic, PE, anxiety/hyperventilation)
Immediate priorities: airway/oxygenation, intramuscular epinephrine first-line, positioning, IV access and fluids, remove/stop trigger
Initial treatment delivered (0.3 mg IM epinephrine via autoinjector, antihistamine, oxygen, fluids) and initial response

sections.description: Explain the biology of anaphylaxis and clarify how biphasic and multiphasic reactions differ from refractory anaphylaxis; introduce mechanisms and contributors relevant to this case, including drug triggers and mast cell disorders.
subtopics: Immunopathology of anaphylaxis: mast cell/basophil activation, mediators (histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes), vascular leak, bronchospasm
Drug-induced anaphylaxis with oral agents: absorption kinetics, potential for ongoing allergen availability without re-exposure
Definitions and distinctions: biphasic vs multiphasic anaphylaxis vs refractory anaphylaxis; clinical implications of each
Proposed mechanisms of biphasic/multiphasic reactions (secondary mediator waves, persistent activation, depot effect)
Tryptase biology and kinetics: timing of peak (~1–2 hours), return to baseline (>24 hours), interpretation of event vs baseline levels
Mast cell disorders overview: systemic mastocytosis pathobiology, why it increases anaphylaxis risk/severity, brief WHO criteria framework and relevance to this patient

sections.description: Detail the investigations, timing, and reasoning that supported multiphasic anaphylaxis, consideration of systemic mastocytosis, and exclusion of mimics or perpetuating factors.
subtopics: Establishing multiphasic course: asymptomatic intervals between discrete relapses without re-exposure; decreasing severity across episodes
Differentiating from sustained anaphylaxis: assessing for ongoing allergen absorption, missed doses, or delayed gastric emptying; absence of new exposures
Tryptase sampling protocol (ideal three-sample strategy) and deviations in this case; interpretation of elevated event and persistently increased baseline tryptase
Workup for mast cell disease: indications to screen (severe anaphylaxis, elevated baseline tryptase), bone marrow biopsy limitations, minor vs major WHO criteria
Review of risk modifiers and comedications: body weight and dosing relevance, absence of ACE inhibitors/beta-blockers, timing of hydrochlorothiazide
Consideration of alternative diagnoses for relapses (sepsis, carcinoid, endocrine causes) and why they were unlikely here

sections.section_title: Acute Management Nuances and Monitoring Strategy
sections.description: Present evidence-based treatment priorities, epinephrine dosing strategy, the role (and limitations) of adjuncts, and approaches to observation/ICU care for multiphasic courses.
subtopics: Epinephrine as first-line: dose 0.01 mg/kg up to 0.5 mg IM in adults; importance of prompt dosing; site and technique
Underdosing pitfalls: 0.3 mg autoinjectors vs 0.5 mg adult dosing; evidence linking lower initial doses to need for escalation
When to escalate: repeat IM epinephrine, IV fluids for hypotension, airway support; indications and cautions for IV epinephrine infusion in recurrent episodes
Adjuncts: antihistamines for cutaneous symptoms only; inhaled beta-agonists for bronchospasm; corticosteroids—current evidence against routine use and potential harms
ICU vs ward monitoring: risk factors prompting higher-level care (severe initial presentation, multiple epinephrine doses, comorbid mast cell disease)
Observation duration and strategies: timing of most biphasic events, risk-stratified observation, triggers for discharge readiness
Case-specific decisions: episodic IM dosing vs contemplated continuous IV epinephrine; rationale for expectant monitoring as severity waned

sections.section_title: Disposition, Long-term Management, and Clinical Lessons
sections.description: Summarize outcomes, secondary prevention, patient education, and practice pearls that translate this case into durable clinical habits.
subtopics: Outcome: cessation of relapses, step-down from ICU, hospital discharge after 3 days
Discharge planning: epinephrine autoinjector prescription and training; consider 0.5 mg device for adults >50 kg where available; written emergency action plan
Trigger avoidance: macrolide caution and clear documentation; no provocation testing given risk and ease of avoidance
Follow-up with allergology/immunology: repeat baseline tryptase, assessment for mast cell disease, counseling on co-triggers (alcohol, heat, NSAIDs)
Chronic symptom control: non-sedating H1 antihistamine (levocetirizine) and tailoring in suspected mast cell disorders

Key takeaways: prioritize correct epinephrine dose early; steroids not routine; obtain properly timed tryptase; risk-stratify monitoring; consider mast cell disorders in severe or atypical courses; research/registry needs for multiphasic anaphylaxis
